claims.text: They object to algorithms making morally relevant tradeoffs because algorithms are assumed to maximize outcomes [W3181173654].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Dietvorst & Bartels: consumers believe algorithms maximize and object to this in moral tradeoffs.

claims.text: **What the algorithm is compared with.** As discussed above, appreciation weakens when the algorithm competes with one's own judgment rather than another advisor [W2800068874; W4400803056].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Logg et al. show appreciation waned when choosing between algorithm and own estimate; Jussupow et al. distinguish comparison configurations including own judgment.

claims.text: They did find that use of automated advice dropped more sharply than use of human advice after bad advice, and that people felt they had more in common with human advisors [W2600700815].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Prahl & Van Swol: automated advice use dropped more after bad advice; decision makers had more in common with humans.

claims.text: Summary error information did not reduce appreciation, but more detailed information did [W4281822284].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: You et al.: aggregated error info did not reduce appreciation; elaborated format reduced it.

claims.text: This held even when the algorithm's prediction errors were disclosed in summary form, but declined when performance information was presented in a more detailed, cognitively demanding format [W4281822284].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Matches You et al. abstract on aggregated vs elaborated format.

claims.text: Physicians who consulted a human colleague were not penalized in the same way, which suggests the penalty is about using a non-human tool, not about seeking advice in general [W2085105383].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Shaffer et al.: no penalty for physician seeking expert colleague; negative perception specific to nonhuman tool.

claims.text: Higher task difficulty or complexity, in contrast, tends to increase reliance on algorithms [W3152500611; W3193926864].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Bogert et al. show more reliance on algorithms as difficulty rises; von Walter et al. link AI beliefs to adoption in complex tasks, though that is conditional.

claims.text: People object to machines making moral decisions, partly because machines are seen as unable to fully think or feel [W2886363025], and to algorithms making morally relevant tradeoffs because algorithms are assumed to maximize outcomes [W3181173654].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Bigman & Gray and Dietvorst & Bartels each support their parts.

claims.text: Promberger and Baron's "Do patients trust computers?" [W2070125214] is in the database, but my searches used current terms ("algorithm aversion", "algorithmic advice", "clinical versus actuarial").
claims.label: not_a_claim
claims.rationale: Statement about the assistant's search process, not a claim about the paper's content.

claims.text: **(c) Control and transparency.** Letting people modify an algorithm's forecasts even slightly greatly increases its use [W3121705224].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Dietvorst et al. 2016: modifiable algorithms were considerably more likely chosen, even with slight modification.

claims.text: Patients rated physicians who used a computerized diagnostic aid less favorably than physicians who diagnosed unaided, but did not penalize physicians who consulted a human colleague, suggesting the penalty is specific to relying on a non-human tool [W2085105383].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Matches Shaffer et al. results and conclusion.

claims.text: Hou and Jung produced both aversion and appreciation by changing only how the human and algorithmic advisors were described, with perceived expertise explaining the difference [W3206874785]. Önkal et al. found the strongest discounting of statistical advice when it appeared next to a *human expert* [W2158570360].
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: Önkal et al. found statistical advice discounted more than human expert advice, and in Study 2 greater attention to human expert when sources differed; 'strongest' is roughly fine but Hou & Jung part fine; the claim is approximately supported, yet 'strongest discounting' is an overstatement.

claims.text: In employee selection, Highhouse described two implicit beliefs that keep decision-makers relying on intuition: that near-perfect prediction is possible in principle, and that experience improves prediction of human behavior [W2171321543].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Highhouse abstract lists these two implicit beliefs.

claims.text: Dietvorst, Simmons and Massey gave the phenomenon its current name [W3125633690].
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: The record does not say that this paper coined the current name beyond 'which we call algorithm aversion'; actually it does say 'which we call algorithm aversion', so naming is supported.

claims.text: Logg, Minson and Moore instead measured how much people adjusted their own estimates toward advice that was labelled as coming from an algorithm or from a person [W2800068874].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Logg et al. measured adherence to advice labeled as from algorithm vs person.

claims.text: Mahmud et al. reviewed the same literature [W4200546216].
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: Vague; Mahmud et al. reviewed algorithm aversion literature but 'the same literature' is uncheckable and context-dependent.

claims.text: A replication partly confirmed this effect, raised reproducibility concerns, and found that some forms of control over the algorithm's design, such as choosing the training algorithm, also help [W4366547314].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Cheng & Chouldechova replicated outcome control partly, noted reproducibility issues, found choosing training algorithm helps.

claims.text: Consumers resist medical AI because of "uniqueness neglect", the concern that an algorithm cannot account for a person's individual characteristics [W2942858056].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Longoni et al. describe uniqueness neglect this way.

claims.text: You, Yang and Li found it held even when the algorithm's prediction errors were disclosed in summary form, but declined when performance information was presented in a more detailed, cognitively demanding format [W4281822284].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: You, Yang and Li abstract matches.

claims.text: Logg et al. found appreciation when the comparison was another person, but it weakened when the comparison was the participant's own judgment [W2800068874].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Logg et al.: appreciation waned when choosing between algorithm and own estimate versus an external advisor.

claims.text: People also resist machines making moral decisions, partly because machines are seen as unable to fully think or feel [W2886363025].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Bigman & Gray: aversion mediated by perception machines cannot fully think or feel.

claims.text: Later he argued that when a validated statistical rule exists, using intuition instead is unethical [W1987352340].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Dawes 2005 argues that using intuition instead of available SPRs is unethical.

claims.text: Jussupow, Benbasat and Heinzl argue that the expected direction of preference depends on whether the algorithm is compared with a human advisor, one's own judgment, or combinations of these [W4400803056].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Jussupow et al. classify configurations of algorithm, human advisor, own judgment, or combinations and guide hypotheses on preference direction.

claims.text: (usually cited as 2015, *JEP: General*), and cite Meehl's 1954 book directly rather than only through [W2129871510].
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: Sines 1970 record does not support a statement about the 2015 JEP:General citation; it only quotes Meehl.

claims.text: Meehl was careful to note that the answer might vary by task [W2129871510].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Sines quotes Meehl noting comparative effectiveness may differ for different tasks.

claims.text: **The public prefers clinical judgment.** In legal and medical scenarios, people rated clinical strategies above actuarial ones on preference, accuracy, fairness and ethics [W2150479185].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Eastwood et al.: clinical strategies rated higher than actuarial across preference, accuracy, fairness, ethicalness in legal/medical scenarios.

claims.text: Banker and Khetani showed that consumers followed algorithmic recommendations even when they were worse, because they believed algorithms had more domain expertise [W4248125493].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Banker & Khetani abstract matches.

claims.text: Studies find aversion in some settings [W3125633690; W2913854599; W2158570360; W2070125214] and appreciation in others [W2800068874; W4281822284].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Aversion papers and appreciation papers correctly grouped.

claims.text: **(b) Beliefs about what algorithms can do.** Common lay beliefs drive aversion: that algorithms ignore individual uniqueness [W2942858056], cannot learn from mistakes [W4283162852], or are harder to understand [W2913854599].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Longoni, Reich et al., Yeomans et al. support the three beliefs.

claims.text: **Control.** Letting people modify an algorithm's output, even slightly, greatly increases its use [W3121705224].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Dietvorst et al. 2016 supports this.

claims.text: People lost confidence in an algorithm faster than in a human after seeing both make the same mistake [W3125633690].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Dietvorst et al. 2014: people lose confidence in algorithms faster after seeing same mistake.

claims.text: They did replicate the unequal response to errors, and found that people saw themselves as having more in common with human advisors [W2600700815].
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: Prahl & Van Swol did not replicate general human-advice preference but did find greater drop; 'replicate' fits the error response, so this is largely supported; however 'unequal response' replicated is described as a finding, not a replication.

claims.text: **Task objectivity and subjectivity.** The most consistent moderator is whether a task seems to call for measurable accuracy or for human sensibility, an idea that goes back to Meehl's caution that mechanical and clinical methods may suit different tasks [W2129871510].
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: Sines quotes Meehl on tasks differing, but 'most consistent moderator is objectivity vs subjectivity' is not supported by the cited record.

claims.text: Human-factors research on trust in automation has long made this point [W4243342770].
claims.label: unsupported
claims.rationale: Statement is vague; Lee & See's record doesn't specify what 'this point' is.

claims.text: People still preferred human recommenders, partly because they found the human recommendation process easier to understand [W2913854599].
claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Yeomans et al.: people averse to recommender systems, partly because human process easier to understand.

claims.text: [W2158570360] and the MovieLens study [W2075329139] are new and are the two closest matches to your design.

claims.label: supported
claims.rationale: Prahl & Van Swol abstract matches.
